newsitem.title: EGYPT: Moslem sheikh rejects scholar apostasy charges.
newsitem.headline: Moslem sheikh rejects scholar apostasy charges.

text.p: The head of Sunni Islam's most respected seat of learning said a Moslem scholar charged by a unit of the organisation with insulting Islam was innocent of apostasy, a crime punishable by death under Islamic law.

The Grand Sheikh of al-Azhar, Mohamed Sayed Tantawi, told the al-Ahram daily newspaper in an interview published on Saturday that he had heard "good things" about Hassan Hanafi, a professor at Cairo University charged by al-Azhar Front for Scholars (AFS) early this month with "rejecting the clear teachings of the Koran".

"I personally have heard only good things about Hassan Hanafi and I declare that he is innocent of all the blasphemy and apostasy charges that have been attributed to him," Tantawi told al-Ahram during a visit to London.

"I am against the idea of calling people apostates without proof and I am also against doubting people's intentions. I have asked people who have attended Hanafi's lectures whether he had insulted Islam and they said that he had not.. Anyone saying that he has done so is speaking on a personal basis."
Cairo-based human rights groups have condemned the AFS charges, saying they gave extremist Moslem groups a green light to kill Hanafi and that they were a setback for civil society.

One group said that condemnation by the AFS spurred Moslem militants trying to transform Egypt into a strict Islamic state to kill secular writer Farag Foda in 1992. The militants also tried to kill Nobel prize-winning author Naguib Mahfouz in 1995 for writing a novel they considered blasphemous.
But Tantawi said that the AFS was set up as a society to provide services for the students at al-Azhar, grouped only two scholars and had no authority to pass judgment.
"I was very surprised to hear the mention of the AFS in this issue...the matter has been referred to the head of the Azhar university who is now investigating the matter," Tantawi added.

Intellectuals in Egypt have compared Hanafi's case to that of Nasr Abu Zeid, a happily married university professor who was told by an Egyptian court that he must divorce his wife after he was convicted of apostasy.
